title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy secondary to rituximab-induced immunosuppression and the presence of John Cunningham virus: a case report and literature review
case_prompt: A 60-year-old man with stage III follicular non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma completed 6 cycles of R-CHOP followed by 6 months of maintenance rituximab. Four months after finishing rituximab, he experienced 6 months of fatigue, personality change, and short-term memory impairment. He also developed apraxia of the upper limbs, ataxia, and a right upper-limb tremor. On admission, he had aprosody of speech, perseveration, and left cortical inattention. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 25/30, with deficits reflecting temporofrontal dysfunction. Screening for tuberculosis, Chlamydia pneumoniae, cryptococcal antigen, syphilis, Coxiella burnetii, hepatitis, HIV, and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease was negative. MRI of the brain with gadolinium revealed T2 hyperintense signal in the right frontotemporal white matter extending across the brainstem to the contralateral medulla, with no enhancement and no mass effect.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. HIV encephalopathy was considered given cognitive decline in an immunosuppressed patient — “Screening for tuberculosis, Chlamydia pneumoniae, cryptococcal antigen, syphilis, Coxiella burnetii, hepatitis, HIV, and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease was negative.”  
2. Primary CNS lymphoma was considered because of his lymphoma history, but imaging findings lacked tumor characteristics — “There was no enhancement, and there was a lack of mass effect.”  
3. Stroke was considered due to focal neurologic signs, but the lesions did not match vascular territories — “Typical radiologic features of PML include multiple areas of white matter demyelination do not conform to cerebrovascular territories…”  
4. Brain tumor was considered as a space-occupying lesion, but MRI again showed no enhancement or mass effect — “lack of mass effect or contrast enhancement.”  
5. CNS vasculitis was included in the differential based on subacute white matter changes — “Differentials for these findings include … CNS vasculitis … and multiple sclerosis (MS).”  
6. Reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome was considered because of white matter signal abnormalities — “Differentials for these findings include … reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy …”  
7. Varicella-zoster virus encephalopathy was considered among viral etiologies but was not supported by CSF screening — “Differentials for these findings include … varicella-zoster virus encephalopathy …”  
8. Multiple sclerosis was considered for demyelinating lesions but was unlikely given the patient’s age, subacute course, and lesion distribution — “Differentials for these findings include … multiple sclerosis (MS).”
